summary: Provides the test plan and results supporting advancement of RFC 2679, the one-way delay metric, along the Standards Track following the process in RFC 6576. It focuses on the metric definitions instead of implementations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a measuring stick is declared official, you test that different rulers agree. This memo reports those tests for a way to measure how long one-way trips take.

questions: how was one-way delay metric validated
what is the one way delay metric
what is the adk test for ippm metrics
subtitle: The test report that checks whether two independent tools read the one-way delay metric of RFC 2679 the same way.

tldr.problem: Performance metric specifications such as RFC 2679 needed a way to advance on the Standards Track, but comparing metric implementations directly was hard because many legitimate sources of variation appear in the results.
tldr.mechanism: Following the process in RFC 6576, the memo tests the metric definition rather than the products. Two independent implementations, NetProbe and Perfas+, measured one-way delay over the same tunneled test path with a network emulator, and the results were compared against limits set in advance.
tldr.outcome: The authors conclude the two implementations produced statistically equivalent results, which supports advancing RFC 2679, with minor revisions suggested for the loss threshold and the list of statistics.

today: RFC 6808 is an Informational document and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents the evidence for advancing RFC 2679 and leaves the revision of that RFC for future action.

sections.title: Why Metrics Need Advancement Tests
sections.content:
The IETF IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) working group has considered how to advance its metrics along the Standards Track since 2001. The original idea was to compare the performance of metric implementations, but that proved hard: results vary for many legitimate reasons, and the metric definitions allow a lot of flexibility in parameters.

The process in RFC 6576 changes the focus. The metric definition, not the implementation, is what gets evaluated. Equivalent test results are taken as evidence that the definition is clear and unambiguous, which the memo calls the metric equivalent of protocol interoperability. The process can also reveal options nobody implemented, so they can be dropped.

This memo carries out that process for RFC 2679, the one-way delay metric. It supplies the test setup, the results for each implementation, an evaluation of each metric specification, and conclusions.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking which stopwatch is best, the testers ask whether the rules for using a stopwatch are clear enough that two different stopwatches give the same answer.

sections.title: The Test Setup
sections.content:
Two implementations were used: NetProbe version 5.8.5 and Perfas+ version 3.1. Both send UDP packets of variable size and can produce Periodic or Poisson sample streams.

The test traffic crosses the Internet inside a Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol version 3 (L2TPv3) tunnel. The tunnel headers hide the test equipment addresses and ports from hash functions that would spread different streams over parallel network resources. At each end, a pair of VLANs is looped back, so streams cross the tunnel twice yet look like one-way tests to the equipment.

A Linux host running the netem network emulator adds controlled delay. Each test used packet rates of 1 pps and 10 pps and IP packet sizes of 64, 340 and 500 bytes, chosen to avoid fragmentation. Streams had at least 300 packets, and periodic streams used 1 second spacing unless noted.

Each implementation also reported its calibration. NetProbe timestamps above the UDP layer and relies on NTP synchronization, while Perfas+ uses GPS synchronization with NTP as fallback. Both report results with a resolution of 1 microsecond.
sections.plainLanguage: The testers sent messages down the same long pipe with two different timers watching, and used a gadget to slow the messages by a known amount, so they knew what answer to expect.

sections.title: Limits on Equivalence Set in Advance
sections.content:
The IPPM working group agreed that the threshold for calling results equivalent must be decided before cross-implementation comparisons. The comparison uses the Anderson-Darling K-sample (ADK) test, which asks whether samples look like they come from one distribution.

The required confidence factor for cross-implementation comparison SHALL be the smallest of a 0.95 confidence factor at 1 ms resolution, or the smallest confidence factor of the two same-implementation comparisons for the same test conditions.

Two corrections are allowed before the comparison. A constant time accuracy error of as much as +/-0.5 ms MAY be removed from one implementation's samples, and a constant propagation delay error of as much as +2 ms MAY be removed, because the two paths could not be made fully identical.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the race, the judges write down how close a tie must be, and how much of a head start difference they will forgive, so nobody can change the rules after seeing the scores.

sections.title: The Four Tests and What They Found
sections.content:
Distribution comparison. Four streams from each implementation were compared. One NetProbe pair failed the ADK criterion, and those streams crossed the path in opposite directions. The combined same-implementation and cross-implementation comparisons passed at P>=0.18, so the memo concludes the two implementations can produce equivalent one-way delay distributions. A further run with emulated delay variation showed that with no variation none of the results passed, while with +/-2.5 ms or more the mean adjusted samples passed.

Loss threshold. With the threshold set at 3 seconds, packets delayed beyond it must be declared lost. NetProbe applies the threshold as post-processing, and Perfas+ has a fixed threshold of about one minute but can apply any threshold the same way. The memo takes the position that post-processing is compliant and RFC 2679 should say so.

Serialization. Raising packet size from 64 to 500 octets raised delay by typically 1.1 to 1.5 ms, much more than the roughly 0.077 ms expected for a link of about 45 Mbit/s, so the field test could not confirm the estimate. Instead the authors checked the implementations and found both include serialization time in the measured delay.

Difference sample. Adding 1000 ms of emulated delay was measured as an increase of 999818 microseconds by NetProbe and 1000007 by Perfas+, within calibration accuracy.
sections.plainLanguage: They ran four kinds of check. The two timers agreed on how long trips take, agreed on when a message counts as too late, and agreed on how much extra time a bigger package takes.

sections.title: Conclusions and Errata for RFC 2679
sections.content:
The memo concludes that the test results support advancing RFC 2679 to the next Standards Track step, because its requirements are clear and unambiguous across two implementations that gave statistically equivalent results.

Two areas need minor revision: the loss threshold text (Section 6.2.3) and the statistics in Section 5 of RFC 2679. Of the four statistics, only Type-P-One-way-Delay-Inverse-Percentile was implemented by neither tool, so it is a candidate for removal or deprecation. The revision should also reference RFC 6703 and consider all open errata. The revised RFC 2679 text was not ready, so approving it was left for future action.

On security, the memo says only that the considerations for any active measurement of live networks apply, and points to RFC 4656 and RFC 5357.
sections.plainLanguage: The judges say the two timers agree well enough, so the rulebook can move up a level, after a couple of small fixes to its wording.
